profile.reading:
This building is identified in mapping data as an Amazon Web Services facility on Bear Creek Parkway in Euless, Tarrant County, Texas, in the Dallas-Fort Worth metro area. The Fort Worth Report has covered the broader Fort Worth-area data center buildout, and DataCenterDynamics has reported on AWS filings for large new Texas data center campuses, including a $1.2 billion project outside Houston, as part of a wider pattern of AWS site-selection filings across the state. This research did not locate a dollar figure, opening date, or capacity figure in state, county, or trade press coverage that is tied specifically to this Euless, Tarrant County building.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no county, state, or trade press source found for this page breaks the Dallas-Fort Worth AWS footprint down to this specific structure.

Amazon is widely reported in trade and business press to acquire and hold United States data center real estate through a subsidiary named Vadata, Inc., rather than directly under the Amazon.com or AWS names, a practice also seen with AWS campuses in Virginia, Ohio, Oregon, and elsewhere. This research did not pull a Tarrant Appraisal District (tad.org) parcel record to confirm Vadata, or another Amazon-linked entity, as the owner of the specific parcel at this coordinate; that county-level confirmation step, which the assignment for this page identifies as the most reliable source for hyperscaler-owned parcels with no public announcement, was not completed this pass and is noted here as follow-up work rather than assumed.

The Dallas-Fort Worth metro is one of the largest data center markets in the United States by existing colocation and hyperscale square footage, hosting large campuses for CyrusOne, Digital Realty, QTS, and other operators in addition to AWS, concentrated particularly in Dallas, Garland, Richardson, and the Alliance corridor in north Fort Worth and Tarrant County. ERCOT, the grid operator for most of Texas including the DFW area, has separately reported rapidly growing large-load interconnection requests from data centers statewide, a trend Texas lawmakers and regulators have responded to with new large-load interconnection rules in recent legislative sessions.

profile.regional_context: Tarrant County and the wider Dallas-Fort Worth metro have drawn active hyperscale and colocation data center investment, with Fort Worth Report tracking existing and proposed sites across the metro as of 2026. Oncor Electric Delivery serves most of the DFW area's transmission and distribution, and has flagged large-load data center interconnection requests as a fast growing category, similar to the pattern seen around AWS's other Texas filings near Houston reported by DataCenterDynamics. Texas offers local and county-level economic development incentive agreements (Chapter 380/381 agreements) that Tarrant County-area municipalities have used to attract large industrial and data center projects.

reading.body:
This is an Amazon Web Services data center in the Fort Worth metropolitan area, part of a region that has become active for hyperscale development in recent years. AWS does not publish specific power capacity, square footage, or technical specifications for individual buildings as stated company policy, so this facility's contribution to AI infrastructure cannot be measured from published sources. The facility's existence and location are confirmed, but no capacity figure can be derived or stated here.

Fort Worth and Dallas-Fort Worth rank among active hyperscale markets in Texas, with reported AWS expansion into the region driven by available land, power infrastructure, and business regulatory environment. Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities and 468.41 MW of published capacity across 18 facilities. This AWS site has no published capacity on record, placing it outside the ranked set of facilities with disclosed megawattage in the state.

The unpublished status of this facility means it cannot be assessed as a discrete constraint on AI scaling or compute availability. If capacity exists here, it is operationally significant to AWS but not visible in the public record this site maintains. Operators choosing to publish specifications enable measurement of regional compute density and grid pressure; AWS's policy choice to withhold facility-level detail leaves this location's role in the AI infrastructure buildout undocumented in the metrics that matter to grid planning.
